```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
```

globalhex works with a *discrete global grid*: a set of cells that covers the
whole Earth with no gaps or overlaps. This vignette introduces grids, cells, and
the functions that move between them.

```{r setup}
library(globalhex)
```

## Grids

A grid is defined by `hex_grid()`. The default, IGEO7, is an equal-area grid of
hexagons in which each cell has seven children at the next finer resolution.

```{r}
grid <- hex_grid()
grid
```

Every function that creates cells takes a `grid` argument that defaults to
`hex_grid()`, so you rarely need to pass it explicitly. The alternative ISEA3H
grid, in which each cell has three children, is available as
`hex_grid("isea3h")`.

### Resolutions

Resolution 0 is the coarsest level. Each step finer divides every cell into
seven, so cells shrink quickly:

```{r}
resolution <- 0:12
n_cells <- 10 * 7^resolution + 2
data.frame(
  resolution,
  n_cells = format(n_cells, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
  area_km2 = signif(510.1e6 / n_cells, 3)
)
```

Because the grid is equal-area, these areas hold everywhere on Earth, from the
equator to the poles.

The grid is built on an icosahedron, so 12 cells at every resolution are
pentagons rather than hexagons. That is why cell operations use the `cell_`
prefix rather than `hex_`: not every cell is a hexagon. Pentagons have five
neighbors instead of six, and globalhex handles them like any other cell.

## Cells

`point_to_cell()` finds the cell containing a point. Coordinates are always
longitude first, then latitude:

```{r}
gainesville <- point_to_cell(c(-82.32, 29.65), resolution = 7)
gainesville
cell_resolution(gainesville)
```

It also accepts a matrix or data frame. Columns named `lon`/`lat` (or `long`,
`lng`, `longitude`, `x`, `latitude`, `y`) are matched by name; otherwise the
first two columns are used. With sf installed, sf `POINT` objects work too.

```{r}
cities <- data.frame(
  name = c("Gainesville", "Nairobi", "Reykjavik"),
  lat = c(29.65, -1.29, 64.15),
  lon = c(-82.32, 36.82, -21.94)
)
cities$cell <- point_to_cell(cities, resolution = 5)
cities
```

Cells are a vector type, so they sit happily in data frame columns, and they
remember which grid they belong to. Cells from different grids cannot be
combined by accident.

### Geometry

`cell_center()` returns the center of each cell, and `cell_boundary()` its
vertices:

```{r}
cell_center(cities$cell)
```

```{r, eval = has_sf}
polygons <- sf::st_as_sf(cities$cell)
polygons
```

## Neighborhoods

`cell_neighbors()` returns the cells sharing an edge. `cell_disk()` returns all
cells within `k` steps, and `cell_ring()` only those exactly `k` steps away:

```{r}
cell_neighbors(gainesville)
cell_disk(gainesville, k = 2)
```

Functions that can return several cells per input always return a tibble with
one row per result and a column recording which input it came from. That holds
for one input or many, so you never have to handle a list.

`cell_distance()` counts the steps between two cells:

```{r}
other <- point_to_cell(c(-82.0, 29.9), resolution = 7)
cell_distance(gainesville, other)
```

## Changing scale

Each cell has one parent at the next coarser resolution, and seven children at
the next finer one:

```{r}
parent <- cell_parent(gainesville)
parent
cell_children(parent)
cell_parent(gainesville, resolution = 3)
```

A cell's ID begins with its parent's ID, so a cell vector can mix resolutions:

```{r}
mixed <- c(parent, gainesville)
cell_resolution(mixed)
```

To summarize values from fine cells into coarse ones, use `cell_aggregate()`,
described in `vignette("plotting")`.

## Saving and restoring cells

A cell ID is a short string of digits. Store it as text, never as a number, or
leading zeros will be lost. After reading it back, attach the grid again with
`as_globalhex_cell()`:

```{r}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(data.frame(cell = as.character(cities$cell)), path, row.names = FALSE)

restored <- read.csv(path, colClasses = "character")
restored$cell <- as_globalhex_cell(restored$cell, grid)
restored
```

`cell_is_valid()` checks that IDs read from elsewhere are well formed:

```{r}
cell_is_valid(c("0200501", "0200509", "99"), grid)
```

## Under the hood

globalhex calls a bundled copy of [DGGRID](https://github.com/sahrk/DGGRID).
`globalhex_info()` reports which copy is in use and the versions of related
packages. To use your own DGGRID build instead, set the `globalhex.dggrid`
option or the `DGGRID_BIN` environment variable.

For grids created with the older [dggridR](https://cran.r-project.org/package=dggridR)
package, `legacy_grid()` provides a limited compatibility path. It is only
used when you ask for it.
